MRSAudio is a large-scale (~500 hours) multimodal spatial audio dataset spanning four real-world components: MRSLife (everyday activities), MRSSpeech (conversational speech), MRSSing (singing), and MRSMusic (instrumental music). It includes high-quality binaural and FOA recordings, synchronized egocentric and exocentric video, 3D motion trajectories, and rich semantic annotations. The paper presents five benchmark tasks to demonstrate the utility of the dataset for spatial audio modeling and generation.
MRSAudio is a technically solid, novel, and high-impact contribution that establishes a new benchmark for multimodal spatial audio research. Minor issues (visual utilization, FOA coverage, bias/fairness) can be addressed in camera-ready revisions.

author_final_remarks.value:
We appreciate the reviewers’ positive assessments and constructive suggestions, with consensus strengths highlighted across reviews:
- **Scale and novelty**(All reviewers): A 500-hour, real-world, multimodal spatial audio dataset spanning four scenarios with rich spatial, linguistic, musical, and event annotations.
- **Multimodal annotation pipeline**(Reviewers WSi9, w87t, jwVD): A reusable semi-automatic pipeline with expert corrections, supporting quality and reproducibility.
- **Accessibility and documentation**(Reviewers vfxr, w87t, jwVD): Public dataset/code, demos, and structured directories enabling reproduction.

Below we address several key questions raised by reviewers:

**Visual modality usage**(Reviewers vfxr, w87t)

Although our paper focuses on spatial audio, we explore visual data utility by integrating visual priors into SELD following STARSS23, which improves localization (e.g., FOA+visuals increases F20° from 9.33 to 13.00). We plan to develop spatial visual-audio generation models in future work and hope our dataset will enable further progress in this area.

**Annotation quality**(Reviewers vfxr, w87t)

We ensure quality through a hybrid annotation pipeline combining automatic tools with manual expert refinement. We randomly audit 15% of all clips. Our experiments demonstrate strong spatial fidelity and audio quality. For example, in SELD, Transformer + FOA achieves ER20° = 0.99 and LR_CD = 87.32.

**Demographics, informed consent, privacy and license**(Reviewer jwVD; Ethics reviewers tvKM, PuXg, 1apA)
- We collect and provide age and gender statistics for recording personnel and annotation teams.
- All participants provide informed consent before recording, and we translate key consent clauses for reviewer reference. 
- Our audio data contains no personal information, and for visual data, we plan to provide only face-masked videos, with full videos available upon special request.
- We initially selected the CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license during dataset creation, but subsequent README edits inadvertently removed the license. We will restore licensing and usage guidelines across all repositories and pursue formal IRB oversight.

We also address other reviewer suggestions regarding recording details, generalization, and citations, which will be updated in the final version. All reviewers who participated in the rebuttal process have indicated that our responses address their concerns. We greatly appreciate the reviewers’ valuable feedback.

Thank you for your thoughtful and rigorous evaluation of the ethical implications. We truly value your concerns regarding data privacy and demographic transparency. We address your comments point by point below:

## 1. Clarification on Informed Consent and Privacy Risk Disclosure

We fully agree that the release of synchronized audio-visual data introduces inherent privacy risks, especially in the era of powerful generative models capable of producing synthetic content. In light of this, our informed consent process goes beyond a standard release form. Specifically, we provide written, signed consent forms to all participants. Due to length constraints, key clauses from original translated forms are listed as follows:

**Researcher Commitments:**
- Purpose of Data Collection: The data, which includes spatial position, voice content, and corresponding video, will be gathered during the entire session.
- Academic Use Only: All collected data is strictly for academic research and will not be used for any commercial or non-profit purposes.
- Anonymization and Privacy: For any publicly released academic research data, the research team will anonymize it to protect personal information. No published research findings will contain personally identifiable information. The team state that while complete anonymization of audio-visual data may not be technically possible, all data will be processed to ensure that individuals are not personally identifiable in any public release.

**Participant Rights, Agreements, and Obligations:**
- Voluntary Participation: Participants confirm they are Zhejiang University students and are participating voluntarily.
- Right to Withdraw: Participants have the right to withdraw from the dataset at any point.
- Consent to Data Publication: Participants agree that the research team can publish the data provided during the recording (including visual and auditory information) in academic papers, with the understanding that their personal identity will not be revealed.

We recognize, however, that traditional consent protocols may be insufficient to fully anticipate future risks such as deepfake misuse. To mitigate these risks further, we implement the following:

- Strict anonymization: All participants wear half-face masks during recording, and camera placement avoids direct facial capture where possible.
- Face masking: In scenarios requiring lip visibility (e.g., audio-visual synchronization), we occlude the eye region, which has been shown to significantly hinder face re-identification accuracy [1].

In the final public release, all videos will have faces fully obscured using either traditional masks or automated anonymization tools such as DeepPrivacy2 [2]. Only upon formal request, submission of a declaration specifying the intended use of the dataset, and signed agreement under ethical usage terms will access to partially masked videos be granted. Applicants requesting data for visual generation tasks must additionally outline specific preventive measures against misuse in their declaration.

## 2. Demographic Transparency and Dataset Fairness

We agree that the ability to audit for fairness and representational bias is critical. Our current participant distribution is as follows:

- **Recording Participants (N=161):** Recruited from multiple departments at Zhejiang University; Age: 18–25; Gender ratio ≈ 3:4 (male:female). Participants include speakers, singers, and performers in MRSSpeech, MRSSing, MRSLife, and MRSMusic.
- **Annotation Team (N=25):** Professional researchers with domain knowledge in music, phonetics, and linguistics; Age: 20–25; Gender ratio ≈ 3:2 (male:female).

We will publish this summary in a dedicated demographic table in the final paper.

## 3. Expanded Discussion in the Limitations Section

We will include a dedicated paragraph in the Limitations section to explicitly acknowledge and reflect on the fairness-related challenges associated with MRSAudio. We will caution that models trained on MRSAudio may exhibit demographic biases. As such, we strongly recommend that future users evaluate model performance on demographically balanced test sets before drawing general conclusions or deploying models in real-world scenarios.

We are grateful to the reviewer for emphasizing the importance of these issues, and we will incorporate this discussion into the final version to support high standards in responsible and inclusive AI research.

**Reference:**

[1] Zhou, L., Chen, Y., Gao, Y., Wang, J., & Lu, H. (2020, August). Occlusion-aware siamese network for human pose estimation. In *European conference on computer vision* (pp. 396-412). Cham: Springer International Publishing.

[2] Hukkelås, H., & Lindseth, F. (2023). Deepprivacy2: Towards realistic full-body anonymization. In *Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF winter conference on applications of computer vision* (pp. 1329-1338).

Thank you very much for your thorough review and constructive feedback regarding the ethical aspects of our work. We deeply appreciate your efforts in raising these important concerns and respond to each point below.
## 1. Regarding the Response to Question 15 in the Checklist

We appreciate your observation regarding the discrepancy between our answers to Questions 14 and 15 in the checklist. Our initial interpretation was that the project focuses on modeling **audio and spatial propagation**, rather than conducting behavioral or psychological studies involving human subjects, which led us to mark Q15 as “N/A.”

In practice, **we obtain signed data usage consent forms from all participants prior to recording**. Due to length constraints, key clauses from original translated forms are listed as follows:

**Researcher Commitments:**

- **Purpose of Data Collection:** The data, which includes spatial position, voice content, and corresponding video, will be gathered during the entire session.
- **Academic Use Only:** All collected data is strictly for academic research and will not be used for any commercial or non-profit purposes.
- **Anonymization and Privacy:** For any publicly released academic research data, the research team will anonymize it to protect personal information. No published research findings will contain personally identifiable information. The team state that while complete anonymization of audio-visual data may not be technically possible, all data will be processed to ensure that individuals are not personally identifiable in any public release.

**Participant Rights, Agreements, and Obligations:**

- **Voluntary Participation:** Participants confirm they are Zhejiang University students and are participating voluntarily.
- **Right to Withdraw:** Participants have the right to withdraw from the dataset at any point.
- **Consent to Data Publication:** Participants agree that the research team can publish the data provided during the recording in academic papers, with the understanding that their personal identity will not be revealed.

Although this project does not undergo formal IRB review, we take data privacy and ethical responsibility seriously and have implemented strict privacy protection protocols throughout the data collection and release process. We fully recognize the importance of formal oversight and will actively seek IRB approval.
## 2. Demographic Information and Limitations

We agree that demographic transparency is vital to assessing dataset fairness and potential bias. Our current participant distribution is as follows:

- **Recording Participants (N = 161):** University students across multiple majors; Age: 18–25; Gender ratio ≈ 3:4 (male:female);
- **Annotation Team (N = 25):** Trained student researchers (Age: 20–25; Gender ratio ≈ 3:2); backgrounds in music, phonetics, and linguistics.

We will include a **demographic summary table** in the final version of the paper and release accompanying metadata (e.g., age group, gender, academic background) with the dataset, subject to participant consent and privacy protection.

**Regarding representational diversity:** we acknowledge that the current dataset does not include participants with physical disabilities. This is a limitation, and we will explicitly state it in the final version.
## 3. License and Usage Guidelines

Thank you for pointing out the inconsistency between the license claim and the actual repositories. We acknowledge this oversight. Although we select the **CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license** during dataset creation on Hugging Face, subsequent edits to the `README.md` unintentionally remove the license badge and associated usage guidance.

Due to the NeurIPS policy, we are currently unable to update the public code and dataset repositories. However, we have already prepared the updates, and will publish them immediately after the review process concludes. Specifically:

- Restore and clearly display the **CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license** in all relevant `README.md`;
- Add a dedicated section on Guidelines for Responsible and Appropriate Use, covering:
    - The dataset is for non-commercial research and educational use only;
    - To preserve participant anonymity, only fully masked-face videos are publicly released;
    - Access to partially masked videos can be requested by email, with a signed ethical usage agreement;
    - Re-identification attempts via visual or auditory cues are strictly prohibited;
    - Applicants requesting data for visual generation tasks must additionally outline specific preventive measures against misuse in their declaration
    - Derived content must clearly credit the original dataset and comply with license terms.

We sincerely thank you again for your detailed suggestions. We are committed to ethical and responsible data stewardship, and will ensure all checklist responses, metadata documentation, and repository content reflect these improvements.

We sincerely appreciate your positive evaluation of our work and your constructive feedback.

**[Q1: Limited use of visual modality]**

Thank you for pointing out the underutilization of visual information in our current benchmarks. As noted in Section 5, although MRSAudio provides synchronized video for all recordings, the current benchmark tasks are primarily designed to evaluate spatial audio modeling. Nevertheless, we have already taken steps to explore the value of visual data.

1. **Incorporation of Visual Features in SELD**: Following the STARSS23 benchmark [1], we validate the utility of visual modality in the Sound Event Localization and Detection (SELD) task. As detailed in Section 4.5 and Table 6, we adopt the SELDnet model proposed by STARSS23 and evaluate its performance with and without visual priors. Results show that integrating visual bounding boxes significantly improves localization recall (e.g., ConvNet + FOA + visuals improves F20° from 9.33 to 13.00), demonstrating the potential of visual information for spatial reasoning.
2. **Limitations and Future Directions**: As discussed in Section 5, we plan to extend MRSAudio toward video-conditioned spatial generation tasks, including video-driven spatial TTS and singing voice synthesis. While recent works such as Both Ears Wide Open [2] and OmniAudio [3] have explored this direction, publicly available training pipelines are still lacking. We hope the release of our high-quality, richly annotated dataset will enable further progress in this area, and we plan to develop end-to-end audiovisual generation models in future work.

**[Q2: FOA audio underrepresented in benchmarks]**

Thank you for highlighting the imbalance in audio formats. We included FOA recordings in MRSAudio to expand the dataset’s applicability to FOA-specific modeling tasks. 
We would like to clarify the following:

1. **FOA Data Scope**: Due to hardware limitations during large-scale data collection, FOA recordings are only captured in the MRSSound(35 hours total, Appendix A.2), captured using Zoom H3-VR microphones. While smaller than binaural data , this exceeds specialized datasets like STARSS23 (7.5 hours, Table 1).
2. **FOA Utility**: We validate FOA’s effectiveness in SELD (Table 6), where FOA inputs outperform binaural audio (e.g., Transformer + FOA achieves ER20∘=0.99  vs. 1.11 for binaural).
3. **Future Plans**: As stated in Section 5, we plan to expand FOA recordings in future iterations of MRSAudio to improve modality balance and support FOA-specific benchmarks, such as Ambisonics-to-binaural rendering. We believe our high-quality FOA data and annotations can facilitate further advances in ambisonics research. 

**[Q3: Annotation accuracy and consistency]**

Thank you for emphasizing the importance of annotation quality. We have taken careful steps to ensure consistency and accuracy:

1. **Hybrid Annotation Pipeline**: As detailed in Section 3.3 and Appendix A.3, we combine automatic tools (e.g., WhisperX, MFA, LyricFA) with manual refinement by domain experts (e.g., using Praat for phoneme alignment; music experts for MIDI corrections).
2. **Expert Auditing**: We randomly audit 15% of all clips for timestamp accuracy, transcription quality, and modality alignment (Appendix A.4). Scenario-specific experts (e.g., linguists for speech, musicians for singing and music) are assigned to ensure relevant expertise.
3. **Residual Tolerance**: While a small number of imperfections may persist, former spatial audio works[4] usually consider an angular error of less than 20 degrees and a distance error of less than 0.5 meters acceptable. We have taken significant care to minimize them through manual correction. As shown in our benchmark experiments, the final outputs exhibit strong spatial fidelity and audio quality. We believe these minor variances are well within acceptable bounds for most spatial audio modeling tasks. If needed in future updates, we are prepared to extend manual verification to the entire dataset.

**[Additional feedback: Annotation tools release]**

We sincerely appreciate your recognition of our annotation framework. To support broader adoption and facilitate community contributions:

- All core scripts including WhisperX-based alignment, MFA phonemization, and LyricFA-based lyric alignment have been made available in our GitHub repository. Detailed usage instructions are provided in the README.md.
- We also offer additional clarifications and implementation details in Appendix A.3–A.4 of the paper. In future updates, we plan to release demo notebooks illustrating key annotation steps (e.g., phoneme refinement, score alignment) to further lower the barrier for reuse and extension.

Thank you for your high recognition and valuable suggestions.

**[W1: About generalization of the dataset]**

Thank you for your insightful question regarding generalization across spatial audio datasets. We address your concerns from three perspectives:

1. **Generalizability of the Audio Format**: MRSAudio adopts binaural audio as its core spatial format [1], which aligns with human auditory perception and is widely used in AR/VR, acoustic analysis, and spatial audio generation tasks. We follow hardware configurations similar to those suggested in [2], ensuring format-level compatibility with both research and application pipelines.
2. **Empirical Evidence of Cross-Dataset Generalization:** To directly evaluate the generalizability of MRSAudio-trained models, we conduct cross-dataset testing using an external spatial audio dataset [3] that was not seen during training. Despite differences in microphone characteristics and room acoustics, our model achieves comparable or better results than a DSP-based spatialization baseline on both objective and subjective metrics:
    |Metric|W-L2 ↓|A-L2 ↓|P-L2 ↓|PESQ ↑|STFT ↓|MOS-Q ↑|MOS-P ↑|
    |-|-|-|-|-|-|-|-|
    |DSP|0.725|0.060|1.584|1.413|2.140|3.87 ± 0.08|3.71 ± 0.12|
    |Ours (MRSAudio)|1.430|0.057|1.567|1.577|1.745|3.91 ± 0.11|3.89 ± 0.07|

3. **Limitations of Simulated and Crawled Data:** Simulation-based datasets often rely on geometric models, simplified sound propagation assumptions, and non-personalized HRTFs [4]. These settings cannot faithfully reproduce occlusion, reverberation, or transient interactions in complex environments. Crawled datasets suffer from inconsistent quality, format variability, and lack of reliable annotations. In contrast, MRSAudio ensures high spatial fidelity and full multimodal alignment through structured, real-world recording and annotation.
While simulation can assist with pretraining, our results show that real-world datasets like MRSAudio remain essential for high-quality spatial learning, especially in challenging or noisy conditions.

**[W2: About diversity and usefulness of video]**

We appreciate your observation regarding the diversity and utility of the video content in MRSAudio. Our response consists of three parts:
1. **Diversity and Realism of Video Content:**

    MRSAudio includes four components with diverse scene settings:
    - **MRSLife** covers board games, cooking, and office activities involving 62 participants, resulting in over 150 hours of natural audio-visual recordings. Events are entirely unscripted and reflect real-life behavior.
    - **MRSSound** includes structured physical activities like kung fu, sports, and kitchen work, with a wide range of acoustic events and spatial variability.
    - **MRSSpeech** includes more than 200 hours of expressive dialogue in four real rooms of varying size and acoustic properties.
    - **MRSMusic** contains over 75 hours of performance videos from 23 traditional, Western, and electronic instruments.

    As shown in Figure 3(c) and Appendix A.5, our recording spaces span small, medium, and large rooms, ensuring environmental variation. All recordings are conducted in real, everyday locations such as kitchens and classrooms, not studio-controlled rooms. We do apply some spatial constraints (e.g., speaker or sound source placement) for annotation purposes, but we do not enforce behavioral or acoustic control.

2. **Detailed Annotation**

    Compared to Sphere360 [5], which uses web-crawled and simulated video with diverse but uncontrolled conditions, MRSAudio offers unified spatial format (binaural and FOA), consistent audio-video alignment, and detailed annotations (transcripts, lyrics, scores, motion trajectories). Unlike Sphere360, our dataset also includes structured speaking, singing, and instrumental tasks, allowing controllable training.

3. **Usefulness of the Video Modality**

    Although the current version of our paper focuses on spatial audio, we already begin to explore the utility of visual data:
    
    - **Sound Event Localization and Detection (SELD)**: In Section 4.5 and Table 6, we follow the STARSS23 benchmark and incorporate visual bounding boxes in the SELD task. Adding visual features improves localization recall, for example, increasing F20° from 9.33 to 13.00 in ConvNet + FOA setups.
    - **Future Work**: As discussed in Section 5, we plan to develop video-conditioned generation tasks such as video-driven spatial TTS and spatial singing voice synthesis. This builds upon recent advances in video-to-audio modeling (e.g., OmniAudio, Both Ears Wide Open[6]), where MRSAudio can provide aligned and richly annotated training material.

    We believe that the visual stream in MRSAudio offers strong potential for cross-modal learning and plan to incorporate it into future benchmarks and generation tasks.

**[W3: About Table 2 and subset-wise training of BinauralGrad]**

Thank you for pointing out this ambiguity. To clarify, in Table 2, each row corresponds to a BinauralGrad model trained and evaluated on one specific subset of MRSAudio. That is, we train a separate model on each subset (MRSLife, MRSSpeech, MRSSing, and MRSMusic) and report its performance on the corresponding test split.

To address your second question, we conduct a new experiment where BinauralGrad is trained on the full MRSAudio training set across all subsets.

|-|-|-|-|-|-|-|-|
|**DSP**|1.691|0.048|1.562|**2.830**|**1.246**|3.89 ± 0.09|3.75 ± 0.11|
|**MRSLife**|0.076|0.025|0.898|-|2.243|3.91 ± 0.07|3.87 ± 0.10|

These results suggest that training on the entire dataset leads to improved generalization and higher perceptual quality. We will include this setting in the updated version of the paper for completeness.

**[W4: About the annotation quality]**

Thank you for your thoughtful question regarding annotation reliability. We implement multiple measures to ensure consistency and reproducibility across all annotation stages.

1. **Manual Annotation:**
    
    - **MRSLife (MRSSound)**: Every audio clip corresponds to a single sound event at a known spatial location. After initial labeling, clips are manually checked for start/end timing and spatial annotation quality. Experts identified and corrected event boundary mismatches.
        
    - **MRSSpeech**: WhisperX and MFA are used for automatic speech-to-phoneme alignment. Experts reviewed clips using Praat to correct phoneme boundaries and ensure speaker turn accuracy.

    - **MRSSing**: Lyrics are aligned with LyricFA and then adjusted by expert annotators with musical training. Note-level MIDI pitch and duration are refined using musician feedback, correcting samples with minor timing or pitch errors.
        
    - **MRSMusic**: Complex polyphonic segments are labeled using pitch transcription tools and further adjusted by professional musicians. Ambiguous notes or overlapping instruments are flagged and manually annotated.
2. **Double Verification:** We conduct double-checking where experts randomly audit 15% of clips (covering all four modules). The auditing process includes four key steps: 1) cross-modal temporal synchronization verification, 2) event label accuracy validation, 3) speech/lyrics-to-audio alignment check, and 4) confirmation of musical properties (pitch, duration, etc.), ensuring high annotation quality (see Appendix "A.4" for details).
3. **Standardization and Reproducibility Protocols:** Each scene or subset is assigned to a dedicated team to ensure consistent labeling styles. Weekly calibration meetings are held to align annotation practices, especially when handling ambiguous or multi-label scenarios. The annotation process and tool usage are documented in detail (see Appendix A.3–A.4), facilitating reproducibility for future contributors.

We will add summary statistics to the appendix. Thank you again for highlighting this important aspect.

**[W5: About the usage of Chinese characters in file names]**

Thank you for your suggestion regarding file naming conventions. To avoid such problems, we ensure that all file names in the released dataset use only ASCII characters. For multilingual content, including Chinese, we store the human-readable names and original script references in a centralized `metadata.json` file, where each entry is linked to a unique alphanumeric ID. This design maintains cross-platform compatibility while preserving full multilingual information for academic use.

[4] Savioja, Lauri, and U. Peter Svensson. "Overview of geometrical room acoustic modeling techniques." *The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America* 138.2 (2015): 708-730.

[5] Liu, H., Luo, T., Luo, K., Jiang, Q., Sun, P., Wang, J., ... & Xue, W. (2025). Omniaudio: Generating spatial audio from 360-degree video. *arXiv preprint arXiv:2504.14906*.

**[Q1: Regarding the realism of the dataset]**

We appreciate the reviewer’s concern regarding the potential lack of realism and robustness in datasets recorded in lab-controlled settings. While some structured planning was necessary for accurate annotation and efficient data collection, MRSAudio was carefully designed to retain natural acoustic complexity and diversity, as detailed below:
1. **Real-world Recording Environments**: All four subsets (MRSLife, MRSSpeech, MRSMusic, and MRSSing) are recorded in authentic indoor settings such as kitchens, classrooms, and studios (see Section 3.2). Certain controlled elements such as predefined speech content, singing lyrics, or musical scores are applied only to support benchmarking and alignment accuracy, without affecting the natural characteristics of the scenes.
2. **Preserved Natural Acoustics**: We intentionally avoid anechoic chambers and retain natural background noise, reverberation, and overlapping events. For instance, MRSLife includes ambient sounds such as footsteps, keyboard typing, or range hood noise. 
3. **Free-form, Complex Interaction**: Many sessions especially in MRSDialogue are conducted with minimal interference, encouraging spontaneous human behavior. For example, kitchen scenarios include multi-layered sound events, such as chopping , boiling water, and wind noise (background), reflecting realistic auditory scenes (see Appendix A.5).
4. **Diverse Scene Dynamics**: We captured spatial variability using head-mounted binaural microphones, varied room sizes (Figure 3c), and dynamic movement in MRSSpeech and MRSLife (e.g., walking while talking, gameplay). These design choices emulate complex, non-stationary acoustic conditions found in real environments.
As a next step, we plan to introduce more dynamic elements such as random interruptions or multi-source overlapping scenes to enhance environmental complexity. 

**[Q2: Regarding fairness and demographic bias]**

Thank you for raising this important point. We fully acknowledge the importance of fairness, demographic representation, and ethical considerations in dataset design. While MRSAudio focuses on spatial and multimodal diversity, we also take active measures to ensure a balanced participant composition:
1. **Performers**: Across all four subsets, we recruit **students from diverse majors** at Zhejiang University. The participant group includes **161 individuals**, aged **18 to 25**, with a **gender ratio of approximately 3 to 4 (male to female)**. 
2. **Annotation Team**: We employ 25 professional annotators (ages 20 to 25, gender ratio 3 to 2, male to female) who conduct fine-grained annotations of transcripts, phoneme boundaries, music scores, and movement descriptors. All annotators are trained student researchers with relevant domain expertise.

We will include a summary of participant demographics in the final version of the paper and ensure that comprehensive metadata, including gender, age group, and academic background, is provided along with the dataset, subject to privacy protection and informed consent.

## Dataset
Thank you for your detailed and constructive feedback regarding the dataset section.. 

**[D1 and D2: About the MRSLife recording]** 

For each sample, we store the exact positions and orientations of all recording devices in a JSON file.

The binaural dummy head is co-located with the egocentric camera and the Zoom H3-VR (Ambisonic recorder). The egocentric camera is rigidly aligned with the head's gaze to capture first-person visuals, while the Ambisonic recorder is mounted 7.5 cm above the head. An exocentric camera is placed at a surveyed position in the scene to provide a third-person view (non-360°)  of the environment and object relationships.

**[D3: About the UWB]**

We use a UWB with anchors placed at surveyed locations and tags attached to sound sources. Moving participants wear tags to record source trajectories. For large and medium scenes, we deploy 8 anchors; for smaller scenes, 6 anchors suffice. Up to 4 tags are used simultaneously in a single scene. Details will be included in the revised appendix.

**[D4: About the demonstration of word cloud]**

We include MRSLife, MRSSpeech, MRSMusic, and MRSSing in Figure 3(b) because we regard *Life*, *Speech*, *Music*, and *Sing* as the highest-level event categories. The relative sizes of these terms are used to emphasize the composition and distribution of the dataset.

**[D5: About the definition of room size]**

We include 12 distinct scenes in the dataset.
For room-size categorization, we define *small* as scenes with a radius of 4-8 m, *medium* as 8-15 m, and *large* for outdoor scenes and for spaces larger than 15 m. We classify scenes and report statistics according to these definitions. We will include this information in the appendix of the revised version.

**[D6: About the audio clips]**

We apologize for the annotation error. In the legend of Figure 3(d), **“MRSLife” should be corrected to “MRSDialogue”**. As described at Line 190, MRSSound was uniformly segmented into 10-second clips; aggregating these clips would concentrate a large number of segments in the 9-10s bin, thereby obscuring the segment-length distribution of MRSDialogue. For this reason, we report MRSDialogue separately. We will correct the legend from *MRSLife* to *MRSDialogue* in the revised version. Thank you for pointing this out.

## Benchmark
Thank you for your thoughtful questions and suggestions regarding the benchmark section. 

**[B1: About the ANG cos and DIS cos]**

We evaluate spatial alignment in the generation task using ANG Cos and DIS Cos. Concretely, both metrics are cosine similarities computed between the angle and distance embeddings, respectively, that are extracted by SPATIAL-AST from the generated audio and from the ground-truth audio. The detailed implementation of these computations is provided in our open-source code repo.

**[B2: About audio spatialization metrics]**

The metrics we used are adapted from the codebase of BinauralGrad[1]. The original references for BinauralGrad may include works such as [2,3,4]. We will include citations to these works in the final version of the paper.

**[B3: About Table 2 Method column]**

As noted in the caption, only the MRSSound portion of MRSLife is included here. Other parts, like MRSDialogue, are grouped under MRSSpeech due to their conversational focus and linguistic richness.
We will clarify this further in the final version to avoid confusion.

**[B4: About Table 2 PESQ]**

The "-" in PESQ indicates not applicable, as MRSLife and MRSMusic contain non-speech audio (e.g., environmental sounds, music), making PESQ unsuitable. Since PESQ is designed for speech quality, applying it here would be invalid.
Instead, we report other metrics like STFT, MOS-Q, and MOS-P, which are more appropriate for general audio quality and spatial perception.

**[B5: About Table 2 DSP]**

Thank you for the insightful question regarding the DSP baseline’s strong performance in PESQ and STFT in Table 2.

Annotation Quality: The strong DSP results support the accuracy of our spatial annotations, showing that even simple rendering benefits from precise label alignment.

Minimal Signal Modification: DSP applies basic spatial cues (e.g., ITD/ILD), causing minimal changes to the original monaural waveform (mainly phase shifts) leading to higher PESQ and lower STFT loss, which favor waveform similarity.

Complexity of Learned Models: In contrast, generation models involve one-to-many mappings and are affected by room variations (e.g., reverberation), producing perceptually valid outputs that may diverge spectrally from the reference, thus scoring lower on PESQ/STFT.

In short, DSP scores better on waveform-based metrics, but subjective MOS reveals that learned models yield more perceptually realistic spatial audio.

**[B6: About difference between MRSDrama and MRSAduio.]**

Compared with MRSDrama, MRSAudio introduces the following extensions:

1. Broader scene diversity. We cover a wider range of environments including meeting rooms, offices, kitchens, and additional outdoor athletic scenarios beyond only three scenes in MRSDrama.
2. UWB trajectory tracking: Unlike MRSDrama’s fixed paths, MRSAudio uses UWB localization to capture free-form source movement with higher positional accuracy.

**[B7: About train/test split and SP method]**

We describe the train/test split in Appendix B.2, Line 625. We randomly sampled 400 examples as the test set. The same split is used for both the mono-to-binaural conversion and the end-to-end generation tasks.

**[B8: About categories in  SELD experiment]**

We modify the STARSS23 baseline code. Since our event taxonomy substantially exceeds the original number of classes in STARSS, we explicitly set num_class = 37 for both training and evaluation, thereby changing the classifier output dimensionality and enabling prediction over all MRSSound categories.

**[B9: About  LR_CD metrics]**

We indeed adopt the macro mode from STARSS23. 

LR_CD indicates the true positive rate—i.e., the proportion of correct localization estimates detected within a given class relative to the total number of instances for that class, which is highly sensitive to both category imbalance and model robustness on fine-grained spatial cues. This naturally introduces greater variance than global metrics.

Transformer models generally outperform ConvNets by better modeling long-range spatial and temporal cues, but they are also more prone to training-induced fluctuations across classes.

The input audio format also plays a role: FOA provides richer spatial information than binaural audio, typically resulting in higher LR_CD scores.

Visual input can help in some cases, but may introduce modality mismatch or redundancy, especially when spatial cues from audio are already strong, leading to reduced or unstable LR_CD in some audio-visual Transformer settings.

Due to space constraints, we report results for a randomly selected 5 classes in the main text of Transformer with FOA without Visual Information as follow.

summary.value:
The paper introduces the MRSAudio dataset, one of the largest and most richly annotated spatial audio datasets.
Using the dataset, the paper constructs five benchmark tasks, ranging from audio spatialization to sound event localization and detection (SELD).
Although the presentation provides an outline, some details are missing from the dataset and the benchmark.

strengths_contributions.value:
* The paper introduces the MRSAudio dataset
  - containing 500-hour recording, i.e., one of the most large-size spatial audio datasets
  - assembling spatial audio data, video data, source positions, transcripts, scores, lyrics, and event labels (i.e., one of the most rich-annotated spatial audio datasets)
* The paper establishes five benchmark tasks from audio spatialization to sound event localization and detection (SELD)

limitations_weaknesses.value:
As for the presentation, some details are missing. The paper can clarify the following points regarding the dataset details.
* L138 MRSLife Recording: How are the binaural head, exocentric cameras, Zoom H3-VR (Ambisonic recorder), and egocentric cameras (GoPro) positioned?
* L138 MRSLife Recording: What is the difference between exocentric and egocentric cameras? Is it a perspective view or a 360-degree view?
* L184 Sound Localization Annotation: How does the paper use the Ultra-Wideband (UWB) system? While it cites a reference, this paper lacks details of the usage.
* Figure 3 Word Cloud: Why MRSLife/MRSSpeech/MRSSing/MRSMusic are included?
* Figure 3 Room Size: How does the paper define Small/Medium/Large?
* Figure 3 Distribution of Clip Durations: In L190, "MRSSound audio is uniformly divided into 10-second segments". However, the value of 10 seconds on the x-axis is not high.

There are also missing details in the benchmark.
* L220 "we compute cosine similarity scores for direction (ANG Cos) and distance (DIS Cos)": How is the cosine similarity used?
* L234 Audio Spatialization Metrics: Are they the same metrics as (Gao & Grauman, 2019), "Visually Informed Binaural Audio Generation without Binaural Audios" or "Cross-modal Generative Model for Visual-Guided Binaural Stereo Generation"? If so, the paper can cite them to clarify its metrics.
* Table 2 Method column: What does "MRSLife" mean here? A BinarualGrad method trained using MRSLife?
* Table 2 "-": What does "-" mean in PESQ?
* Table 2 DSP: Do the authors have any idea about why DSP performs better in PESQ and STFT?
* L248 ISDrama (i.e., the MRSDrama dataset): The paper should mention the difference between MRSDrama and MRSAduio.
* Table 4: The paper can clarify the details of the train/test split and the SP method in this experiment.
* Table 6: How many categories does the SELD experiment use? Figure 5 in the Appendix displays over 20 classes in MRSSound.
* Table 6: Why do LR_CD metrics vary a lot among models? I think the paper follows macro mode computation (i.e., averaging each class's LR) in the STARSS23 dataset. How about micro computation that is used in DCASE2021 Task3 (e.g., https://github.com/sharathadavanne/seld-dcase2021)? The paper could also show class-wise LR results in the appendix for more clarification.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

additional_feedback.value:
* L23 "Dongchao Yang": "Yang et al."
* L75 understanding(Chu, L99 STARSS23(Shimada, and others: They seems no space.
* L117 ", ,": removing
* L138 "Audio": "audio"

* L25 "The human binaural system uses interaural time differences (ITD) and interaural level differences (ILD) to localize sound in three-dimensional space": The paper could add a reference for this sentence.

* Table 1: If space permits, the paper could add "RealMAN: A Real-Recorded and Annotated Microphone Array Dataset for Dynamic Speech Enhancement and Localization" for a multichannel recorded speech type dataset with position labels.

* L161 MRSLife annotation: Just for confirmation. While MRSDialogue records conversations and spontaneous action sounds, it has no annotations of event categories and time intervals for these action sounds. Is it correct?

final_justification.value:
The rebuttal solves the missing details on datasets and benchmarks.
I raise the score from "borderline accept" to "accept".

summary.value:
This submission proposes a new benchmark suite for multi-modal spatial audio analyses and generation. 
The dataset covers four audio-recording scenarios: speech, daily-life sounds, music and songs with 500-hour recordings in total. 
The annotation process is semi-automatic: for example, transcriptions were first generated with WhisperX speech recognition model and then improved with human auditing.
To demonstrate the dataset's usability, five tasks of (i) audio spatialization, (ii) spatial text-to-speech, (iii) spatial singing voice synthesis, (iv) spatial music generation, and (v) sound event localization and detection (SELD) are conducted. The results show successful training of existing baseline methods using the proposed datasets.

strengths_contributions.value:
- The proposed dataset is large-scale and considers practical use cases. The effort to create video-audio data with multiple actors, instruments, recording setup in various controllable settings is highly valuable for the research community.
- Semi-automatic data annotation process is detailed and sophisticated. I realized the power of modern AI tools enabling efficient data curation reading this manuscript.
- The dataset hosting is ready for use by researcher, providing demos and well-structured data directories.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
- Generalization from/to other datasets are not discussed:  recording spatial audio needs specific setup such as microphone arrays, and generalization across the setup is desired but hard. Does MRSAudio generalizes from or to existing datasets, especially ones constructed by crawling or simulations?  If the generalization is not possible, the value of the dataset as a training source would be limited. At the same time, generalization from simulation-based training datasets is possible, we may not have needed a costly long recording for training data.
- Unlike Sphere360 (Liu et al., 2025) the diversity and realism of the video look limited because the most of the videos look to be taken in a recording room. This may be a limitation of the dataset. The usefulness of the videos in MRSAudio is totally not experimented.
- Table 2: In the leftmost column, dataset names are listed in "Method" column and misleading. Does this table means that BinauralGrad network trained on each subset MRSLife--MRSMusic? What happens if BinauralGrad is trained using the whole MRSAudio?
- How often does the human auditing find and correct auto-annotation errors? The statistics about workload would be useful to assess the data reliability and reproducibility.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

ethical_comments.value: While the dataset includes personal data of voices and videos, the Authors clarified the the all participants signed consent forms of the open-source release of their audio and video under the CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license.

dataset_code_comments.value:
I checked the repository uploaded at https://huggingface.co/datasets/verstar/MRSAudio and demo mp4 files at https://mrsaudio.github.io/DataSet%20Page/speech.html .
Comments: 
- I recommend not using non-latin characters in file names; off-course usage of Chinese characters in the transcripts is unavoidable for the multi-lingual dataset, but the usage in file names may cause serious troubles in Linux systems of latin-alphabet-based users.

final_justification.value:
I appreciate the Authors' response. My concerns were not serious originally but are nicely answered. I keep my rating at Accept.
I recommend updating the camera-ready supplementary material to incorporate the new data in the rebuttal, as it will be useful for readers.

summary.value: This paper presents MRSAudio, a large-scale (500-hour) multimodal spatial audio dataset designed for spatial audio understanding and generation. The dataset encompasses four key components in real-world scenarios: MRSLife, MRSSpeech, MRSMusic, and MRSSing, and includes data of synchronized spatial audio, egocentric video, motion trajectories, and annotations of 3D pose, semantic labels. To demonstrate the utility and generalizability of the dataset, the authors conduct five distinct tasks.

strengths_contributions.value:
- This work is the first to introduce a large-scale spatial audio dataset with multimodal alignment, setting a new benchmark for the field.
- The dataset is highly diverse, covering four distinct components that reflect real-world scenarios. The 3D distribution of sound source positions is notably varied.
- The dataset provides high-quality audio and 3D geometry annotations, along with detailed semantic annotations and motion description prompts, which are valuable for a wide range of tasks in spatial audio research.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
- Many settings used to create the dataset are controlled laboratory environments, resulting in overly clean data that may lack robustness and realism for mimicking complex, unpredictable real-world scenarios.
- The paper lacks consideration of dataset bias and fairness, such as representation across different demographics (e.g., ethnicity).

ethical_considerations.value: Yes, there are ethics concerns that require attention by the authors

ethical_comments.value: The dataset includes both audio and video data, which necessitates careful measures to protect human privacy and ensure compliance with ethical standards. Additionally, considerations of bias and fairness need to be addressed, as the dataset's statistics do not include information such as demographic representation. Incorporating demographic data and ensuring diversity in the dataset would help mitigate potential biases and improve fairness in its application.

dataset_code_comments.value: The code has been uploaded to GitHub (https://github.com/MRSAudio/MRSAudio_Main) and is largely complete.

final_justification.value: Thank you for your response! Most of my concerns have been addressed. I raised my rating to "Accept".

title.value: MRSAudio: A Large-Scale Multimodal Recorded Spatial Audio Dataset with Refined Annotations

TLDR.value: This paper presents MRSAudio, a large-scale multimodal recorded spatial audio dataset with refined annotations, designed for spatial audio generation and understanding tasks, along with its benchmarks.

abstract.value:
Humans rely on multisensory integration to perceive spatial environments, where auditory cues enable sound source localization in three-dimensional space. 
Despite the critical role of spatial audio in immersive technologies such as VR/AR, most existing multimodal datasets provide only monaural audio, which limits the development of spatial audio generation and understanding. 
To address these challenges, we introduce MRSAudio, a large-scale multimodal spatial audio dataset designed to advance research in spatial audio understanding and generation. 
MRSAudio spans four distinct components: MRSLife, MRSSpeech, MRSMusic, and MRSSing, covering diverse real-world scenarios. 
The dataset includes synchronized binaural and ambisonic audio, exocentric and egocentric video, motion trajectories, and fine-grained annotations such as transcripts, phoneme boundaries, lyrics, scores, and prompts.
To demonstrate the utility and versatility of MRSAudio, we establish five foundational tasks: audio spatialization, and spatial text to speech, spatial singing voice synthesis, spatial music generation and sound event localization and detection. 
Results show that MRSAudio enables high-quality spatial modeling and supports a broad range of spatial audio research.
Demos and dataset access are available at https://mrsaudio.github.io.
